overview: This two-page file concerns Japanese zinc smelting and a request for information about measures used to control sulfur fumes released from smelter stacks. The first page is a subject note referring to a Tokyo instruction of November 19; the second is an internal State Department memorandum recording a telephone conversation about the Tokyo Embassy’s telegram No. 2 of January 7, 1934, and the possibility of Department assistance to an unnamed company.

people.name: Mackay
people.role: State Department representative who relayed the substance of a Tokyo Embassy telegram

people.name: Dundas
people.role: Representative associated with the unnamed company requesting assistance

subfiles.title: Note on control of sulfur fumes from Japanese zinc smelters
subfiles.about: A filing note records a request for information about Japanese practices for controlling sulfur fumes discharged from zinc-smelter stacks.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies the subject as the manufacture of metals in Japan and refers to a Tokyo instruction dated November 19. It seeks information on measures used in Japan to control sulfur-bearing gases emitted during zinc-ore smelting.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of telephone conversation between Mackay and Dundas
subfiles.about: The memorandum records a telephone conversation concerning a request for Department assistance mentioned in a Tokyo Embassy telegram.
subfiles.summary: Mackay conveyed to Dundas the substance of the first paragraph of the Tokyo Embassy’s telegram No. 2 of January 7, 1934. He said the Department was considering the suggestion in that paragraph and would communicate its decision soon. Dundas replied that the unnamed company would appreciate the proposed assistance but would understand if the Department declined.

interest: The file provides a compact example of how the State Department handled a private commercial or technical inquiry through diplomatic reporting and internal telephone coordination. It is particularly useful as early evidence of interest in industrial air-pollution controls—specifically sulfur emissions from zinc smelting—in Japan. The surviving material is fragmentary, since the referenced Tokyo instruction and telegram are not included, but it reveals the administrative chain connecting an industrial concern, the Department, and the embassy.
